facets.text: A old frontier town near the Borgo Pass, the post town named by the Count, with a stormy history of fires and sieges.

Bistritz is an old frontier town in Transylvania, reached after dark, which the narrator finds interesting and steeped in a stormy past of fires, sieges and losses. It is where Count Dracula directed Jonathan Harker to stay, at the Golden Krone Hotel, and the local people there seem to fear the journey ahead.

Bistritz is an old frontier town in Transylvania, close to the Borgo Pass, with a stormy past of great fires and a long siege. Its people are described as wary of the traveller's journey, and the Golden Krone Hotel there is where the narrator is directed to stay.
The mountain range where Harker now finds himself, the region he has travelled into.

Carpathians is a mountain range in eastern Europe, the wild, lofty region through which Jonathan Harker travels toward Count Dracula's domain. The passages present it as a place of towering forests, snowy peaks, and deep passes such as the Borgo Pass, where local people hold many superstitions about it. Its inhabitants, including Szekelys and Slovaks, are described as living among its valleys.
Mina is someone the diarist plans to talk over his travels with, and whose possible reading of his journal he imagines. The passages show no other tie, look, nature or abilities for her.

Mina is the diarist's sweetheart, someone he plans to talk over his travels with and whose possible reading of his journal he imagines. The passages show no other tie, look, nature or abilities for her.

Mina is the diarist's sweetheart, a woman he hopes to share his travels with and whose eventual reading of his journal he worries about. The passages show her only as a woman he writes to in shorthand and addresses his farewells to; they give no look, nature or abilities for her.

Mina Murray is a young woman who writes shorthand and works as an assistant schoolmistress, and she is the sweetheart of Jonathan, whom she expects to marry. She is Lucy Westenra's close friend, and the two have shared their secrets since childhood. She is practising shorthand and typewriting so she can help Jonathan with his work, and she keeps a journal of her own.
Mina has been staying with Lucy, keeps a diary, and is anxious about Jonathan; she is practical and protective of Lucy.

Mina Murray is a young woman who writes shorthand and works as an assistant schoolmistress, practising shorthand and typewriting so she can help Jonathan with his work. She is Lucy Westenra's close friend, and the two have shared their secrets since childhood. Jonathan, the man she expects to marry, is away in Transylvania, and she keeps a private journal of her own.

Mina Murray is a young woman who writes shorthand and works as an assistant schoolmistress, practising shorthand and typewriting so she can help Jonathan with his work. She is Lucy Westenra's close friend, and the two have shared their secrets since childhood. Jonathan, the man she expects to marry, is away in Transylvania, and she keeps a private journal of her own. In these passages she is also writing as Mina Harker, which shows she has married Jonathan by the time of her later letter.

Mrs. Harker is a letter-writer and diarist who keeps a journal and corresponds with Van Helsing. She is practical and devoted, offering to transcribe papers and to comfort Jonathan. She sends for Van Helsing and records his visit.

Mina is a young woman who writes shorthand and types, and she is an assistant schoolmistress who practises these skills so she can help Jonathan with his work. She is Lucy Westenra's closest friend, and the two have shared their secrets since childhood. Jonathan, whom she expects to marry, is away in Transylvania, and Mina keeps a private journal of her own.

Mrs. Harker is Jonathan Harker's wife, a sensible, sweet-faced young woman who keeps a diary and typewrites papers, including Van Helsing's and Dr. Seward's accounts, to gather the evidence in order. She is devoted and practical, tending to her husband's nerves and welcoming the professor's guidance. She meets Dr. Seward at the station and grieves over Lucy's fate.

Mina is a young woman, an assistant schoolmistress, who is Lucy Westenra's closest friend and expects to marry Jonathan. She writes shorthand and types, and keeps a private journal in which she records her travels and thoughts. Later she is called Mina Harker and Madam Mina.

Mrs. Harker is Jonathan Harker's wife and a young, sweet-faced, dainty woman who keeps a diary and works at a typewriter, copying papers and putting the evidence in order. She is practical, sensible and quietly sympathetic, and she is pained by the loss of Lucy. Dr. Seward finds her attentive and gentle, and Dr. Van Helsing regards her as remarkably clever.

Mina is a young woman and assistant schoolmistress, the closest friend of Lucy Westenra and the intended wife of Jonathan Harker, later Mina Harker. She is careful and capable: she writes shorthand, types, and keeps a private journal of her travels and thoughts. Dr. Van Helsing addresses her as Madam Mina and treats her with great respect.

Mrs. Harker is Jonathan Harker's wife, a sweet-faced, dainty young woman who types and keeps a diary. She works with her husband to copy and order the papers and evidence. Dr. Seward finds her gentle and appealing, and Dr. Van Helsing considers her clever, with a man's brain and a woman's heart.
Has pledged she will not take her own life and will strive to live, while the Count remains alive.

Mrs. Harker is Jonathan Harker's wife, a sweet-faced, dainty young woman who types and keeps a careful record. She and her husband copy and arrange the papers and diaries, and Dr. Seward finds her gentle and appealing. Dr. Van Helsing regards her as clever, with a man's brain and a woman's heart, and wants her kept out of the dangerous work.

Mrs. Harker is Jonathan Harker's wife, a sweet-faced, dainty young woman with a quick, careful mind for records. She types and arranges the diaries and papers, and her gentleness and composure draw Dr. Seward and others to her. Dr. Van Helsing values her clever mind and warm heart and wants her kept out of the dangerous work.
Under hypnosis, speaks in a sad dreamy voice unlike her usual manner, as the Professor questions her.
Falls into a trance-like state in which she describes a ship's sounds and movements, and wakes not remembering what she said.

Mina is a careful, capable young woman and the wife of Jonathan Harker, known as Mina Harker. She writes in shorthand and keeps a private journal, and Dr. Van Helsing addresses her as Madam Mina with great respect. She is a close friend of Lucy Westenra and is treated by the men around her as someone to be shielded from the dangerous work they undertake.
Is changing toward the vampire's traits, with sharper teeth, harder eyes and a growing silence, and is kept from the group's plans.
Insists on travelling with the group, believing she is safer with them and that they will be safer with her.
Says that when the Count wills her she must go to him, and that she may be made to hide her actions even from Jonathan.
Feels something lifting from her and is brighter and more like her old self than she has been for a long time.
Her written memorandum is trusted by the group, and Van Helsing calls her their teacher for her clear reasoning.
Is calm within the protective ring and is held back by the narrator from the fire, while the wheeling figures circle outside.
The Count's castle, whose exact location Harker cannot find on any map in London.
Its doors are all locked and bolted, leaving the castle a prison with exits only through its windows.

Castle Dracula is the place the Count names as his home in the Carpathian mountains, in the far east of Transylvania near the borders of three states. It is a remote, little-mapped site, and the narrator has found no map giving its exact location.

Castle Dracula is the home the Count names in the Carpathian mountains, in the far east of Transylvania near the borders of three states. It is a remote, poorly mapped place, and the narrator has not been able to find a map giving its exact location. Jonathan Harker, a visitor there, later describes it as a place of terrible experiences.
Has a strong aquiline face, pale with extraordinary pallor, sharp white teeth, pointed ears, and coarse hands with hair on the palms.
Has been master for a long time among the common people and wishes to learn English speech and intonation from Harker.
Casts no reflection in the shaving glass, though he stands close behind Harker.
Asks Harker detailed questions about English law, solicitors, banking and shipping, showing deep knowledge of business matters despite never having lived in England.
Can climb down the sheer castle wall headfirst like a lizard, crawling face down with his cloak spreading like wings.
Has dressed in Harker's travelling clothes and carries the bag, to be seen by locals as Harker.
Appears to lie dead or asleep in an earth-filled box, with open stony eyes, warm pale cheeks and red lips, showing no breath or pulse.
Lies in his box gorged with fresh blood, looking rejuvenated, with darkened hair and a malicious grin.

Count Dracula is a nobleman of Transylvania, living in a remote castle in the Carpathian mountains, who corresponds with Jonathan Harker by letter and arranges his travel. The people of Bistritz know of him and show fear when his name is raised, refusing to speak of him or his castle. He is courteous in writing and says he is anxiously expecting Harker.

Count Dracula is a Transylvanian nobleman who lives in a remote castle in the Carpathian mountains and corresponds with Jonathan Harker by letter, arranging his travel. Locals fear his name and refuse to speak of him or his castle. He is courteous, speaks warmly and at length, and in person stays up late chatting with Harker. He has a strong handshake, shows an interest in English maps and books, and is said to have an unusually shrill, supernatural-seeming cock crow nearby at dawn, which Harker notes.

Count Dracula is a Transylvanian nobleman, a boyar of ancient pride, who lives alone in a remote castle in the Carpathians and keeps no servants. He writes courteously to Jonathan Harker, arranges his travel, and holds him as a prisoner. He is courteous and talkative, speaks with great feeling about his house and the history of his land, and has a powerful grip, a white moustache, and sharp canine teeth. Locals fear him and refuse to speak of him, and he is said to command wolves with a raised hand.

Transylvania is a region in the Carpathian mountains, described as an extreme eastern district of its country and one of the wildest, least-known parts of Europe. Its people include Saxons, Wallachs, Magyars and Szekelys, the last of whom claim descent from Attila and the Huns. The narrator notes it as a place steeped in superstition.

Transylvania is a mountainous region in the east of its country, among the Carpathians, and one of the wildest and least-known parts of Europe. Its people are Saxons, Wallachs, Magyars and Szekelys, and the Szekelys claim descent from Attila and the Huns. The narrator finds it steeped in superstition, and the Count speaks of its history with great pride.

Transylvania is a wild, mountainous region in the east of its country, among the Carpathians, and one of the least-known parts of Europe. Its population includes Saxons, Wallachs, Magyars and Szekelys, and the narrator finds it steeped in superstition. The Count speaks proudly of its history and of his race's warlike past.

Transylvania is a wild, mountainous region in the east of its country, among the Carpathians, and one of the least-known parts of Europe. It is home to four nationalities, with the Szekelys, said to descend from Attila and the Huns, living in the east. Its people are steeped in superstition, and the Count speaks with pride of its warlike history and his race's glory there.

Slovaks are a people of the Carpathian region met on the road into Transylvania. They are described as wild-looking, with long black hair, heavy moustaches, sheepskins and big leather belts studded with brass nails, yet said to be harmless and lacking in self-assertion. Some ride in peasant carts or kneel at roadside shrines.

Slovaks are a rough, barbarian-looking people of the Carpathian region, with wide hats, sheepskins, high boots and great nail-studded leather belts. They wear long black hair and heavy moustaches, and are said to be harmless and lacking in self-assertion. They travel with the Szgany on leiter-wagons, handling heavy empty boxes, and serve the Count's household work.

Slovaks are a rough, barbarian-looking people of the Carpathian region, with wide hats, sheepskins, high boots and huge nail-studded belts. They have long black hair and heavy moustaches, and are described as harmless and lacking self-assertion. They handle the heavy empty boxes on the leiter-wagons, work for the Szgany, and are said to be the carriers who move the boxes of earth; one Slovak, Petrof Skinsky, is said to deal with river trade to the port at Galatz.
A mountain pass leading from Bistritz into Bukovina, where the Count's carriage is to meet Harker.
Harker's coach enters the Pass at night, where the mountains seem to close in and the passengers grow tense.

Borgo Pass is a mountain pass in the Carpathians, leading from the frontier town of Bistritz into Bukovina. At night it is a dark, steep route through pine and beech woods, where the passengers grow tense and make the sign of the cross as they enter it.

Borgo Pass is a mountain pass in the Carpathians, the route from the frontier town of Bistritz into Bukovina. Travellers enter it at night through steep, dark woods, grow tense, and make the sign of the cross; a carriage is expected there to meet the arriving Englishman, though it does not appear.

Borgo Pass is a mountain pass in the Carpathians, the route between Bistritz and Bukovina. Travellers pass through it at night, and a carriage is expected there to meet the arriving Englishman, though none appears. Later, a party led by Van Helsing and Mina reaches it at dawn, and Mina seems to know the way ahead.
An old-fashioned hotel in Bistritz where Harker stays and receives a letter from the Count.
An English young man, a churchman by upbringing, who travels to Transylvania on business and keeps a shorthand journal. He is practical, curious and skeptical of the local superstitions.

Jonathan Harker is the English visitor and narrator who arrives at Bistritz and is expected at the Golden Krone Hotel, where he gives his name as Jonathan Harker. He is a lawyer's man working on property affairs for the Count, handling the purchase of an estate at Purfleet and the papers that go with it. He is courteous and curious, taking an interest in local customs and records, and he is the one who conducts the business for the Count.

Jonathan Harker is the English visitor who arrives at Bistritz and gives his name at the Golden Krone Hotel. He handles property and legal papers for Count Dracula, including the purchase of an estate at Purfleet, and is courteous and curious about local matters. Mina writes to him as Jonathan, and he is described as studying and keeping a shorthand journal of his travels abroad.

Jonathan Harker is an English visitor and a careful, courteous man who keeps a shorthand journal of his travels. He is engaged to Mina Murray, who calls him Jonathan, and he handles legal and property papers, including an estate purchase at Purfleet, for Count Dracula. He is also said to be a student of law, working in Exeter with Peter Hawkins.

Jonathan Harker is an English visitor and a careful, courteous man who keeps a shorthand journal of his travels. He is engaged to Mina Murray, who writes of him with affection and worry. He is also a legal man, handling papers for Count Dracula and working with Peter Hawkins in Exeter.

Jonathan Harker is an English visitor and a methodical, courteous man who keeps a shorthand journal of his travels. He is engaged to Mina Murray, who writes of him with affection and worry. He handles legal papers, dealing with Count Dracula's estate purchase and working with Peter Hawkins, who is his associate.

Jonathan Harker is an English visitor and a methodical, courteous man who keeps a careful journal. He is engaged to Mina Murray, who writes of him with love and growing worry. He works on legal and property matters with Peter Hawkins, his associate, and is at times away from home and out of contact.
Was under the care of a Buda-Pesth hospital for nearly six weeks with a violent brain fever, and is recovering there.
Has asked Mina never to learn a secret from his recent past, which he believes may have been real or the dreaming of a madman.
Has taken a new position of responsibility and works away from home for long days.

Jonathan Harker is an English visitor and a methodical, courteous man who keeps careful notes. He is engaged to Mina Murray, who worries about him, and he works on legal and property matters for Mr. Hawkins. At this point he has been ill and out of contact, and he is recovering under the care of a nurse in Buda-Pesth.

Jonathan Harker is an English visitor and a methodical, courteous man who keeps careful notes and a shorthand journal. He is engaged to Mina Murray, who writes to him and keeps watch over his silence, and he is linked to Mr. Hawkins, who passes news of him along. He has been ill, and a Sister at a hospital in Buda-Pesth writes of his care.

Jonathan Harker is an English visitor and a careful, courteous man who keeps notes and a shorthand journal. He is engaged to Mina Murray, who writes to him and worries over his silence. He has been ill, and a Sister at a hospital in Buda-Pesth writes of his care. He is linked to Mr. Hawkins, who passes news of him along.

Mr. Harker is a clever, energetic young man whose face and manner, as Dr. Seward describes them, suggest a businesslike gentleman of considerable nerve. He is linked to Mrs. Harker, with whom he works on gathering and ordering evidence. He is also the one who went down into a vault a second time and is said to have written an account of it. He arrives at the house at nine o'clock, having received a wire from his wife just before setting out.

Mr. Harker is a young, clever, energetic man, who arrives at the house at nine o'clock after receiving a wire from his wife. He is businesslike in manner and, by one account, a man of considerable nerve. He works alongside Mrs. Harker, gathering and ordering evidence, and is also a solicitor who acts on behalf of Lord Godalming.
Rulers of the region in the past, said to have left the roads unrepaired.
The green, hilly country through which the road runs before the mountains rise.

Mittel Land is a region of green, rolling hills, forests and orchards in blossom, lying between the traveller's road and the high Carpathian mountains. It is a countryside rather than a person, seen from a carriage as a land of gentle slopes with pine woods running down the hillsides.
A snow-capped mountain peak in the Carpathians, named by a fellow passenger as 'God's seat'.
Peasant people of the Carpathian region, seen on the road in picturesque dress wearing white sheepskins.

Calèche is a horse-drawn carriage, not a person, that appears in these passages as the vehicle used to collect the narrator from the coach at the Borgo Pass. It is pulled by four black horses and is driven by a tall, strange man who takes the narrator's luggage and guides him through the night. The calèche is later seen to carry him through wolf-filled roads to a ruined castle.
A German ballad whose line a passenger whispers, hinting at the supernatural.
The plum brandy of the country, kept in a flask under the carriage seat.

Mr. Hawkins is a man of Exeter, a friend of Jonathan Harker's and of the Count, who works with them on legal papers and the London property. He is absent from the passages and is never shown acting in person; he is known to the Count through a letter, in which he is described as a gout-free but travel-bound correspondent who sends a substitute. He is the Count's 'friend Peter Hawkins'.

Mr. Peter Hawkins is a solicitor of Exeter, a friend of Jonathan Harker and of the Count, who handles legal and property business with them. He is never seen in person; the Count knows him only through correspondence and through the papers Harker takes to and from him. He is the Count's 'friend Peter Hawkins'.

Mr. Peter Hawkins is a solicitor of Exeter and a friend of Jonathan Harker and of the Count, handling legal and property affairs for them by letter and through papers. He is never met in person. Mina writes to him and receives news of Jonathan from him, and he is described as kind.

Mr. Peter Hawkins is a solicitor of Exeter, a friend of Jonathan Harker and of the Count, and a kind man who handles legal and property affairs by letter. He is never seen in person and is described as gentle and generous. He takes Jonathan into partnership and leaves the couple his fortune, and his firm is Hawkins & Harker.
An English railway timetable the Count is found reading in the library.
A place in England where Harker has found an estate the Count wishes to buy, located on a by-road.

Purfleet is a place rather than a person: a by-road locality where a large, walled estate called Carfax stands, with a long-neglected house, an old chapel nearby, and a deep pond fed by springs. The writer found it for sale and is buying it, to be settled through Mr. Hawkins.

Purfleet is a place: a by-road locality where a large, walled estate called Carfax stands. The estate has an old house with a stone keep-like section, an adjoining chapel, and a pond fed by springs. The house is kept empty and its goods are to be delivered there, and the Harkers are at home at Purfleet.
An estate of about twenty acres near Purfleet, walled and containing an old house, chapel and dark pond.
The Count has used the Piccadilly house as well, with eight of the nine earth-filled boxes found there.

Carfax is an old estate near Purfleet, surrounded by a high stone wall and overgrown with trees, with a large, partly ruined house of many periods. Its four-sided house takes its name from a corruption of an old phrase, and a stone part resembles a keep with an old chapel beside it. The house stands empty and is up for sale, and goods are to be delivered there, kept in the ruined chapel.

Carfax is an old, walled estate near Purfleet, with a large, partly ruined house of many periods and about twenty acres of gloomy trees and a dark pond. Its four-sided house gives the estate its name, a corruption of an old phrase. A thick stone part resembles a keep, beside an ancient chapel, and the house stands empty and for sale.

Carfax is an old, walled estate near Purfleet, with a large, partly ruined house of many periods and roughly twenty acres of gloomy trees and a dark pond. Its name is said to be a corruption of an old phrase about the four-sided house. A thick stone part resembles a keep beside an ancient chapel, and the house stands empty and for sale.

Carfax is an old estate near Purfleet, walled and gloomy, with a large, partly ruined house whose thick stone part resembles a keep beside an ancient chapel. It stands empty, unrepaired and neglected for many years. Its name is said to be a corruption of an old phrase about the four-sided house.

Carfax is an old, walled estate near Purfleet, long unrepaired and gloomy. It has a huge, partly ruined house with a thick stone section like a keep beside an ancient chapel. It has stood empty for years, and it is where a large consignment of earth-filled boxes was delivered and stored.
A place on the Yorkshire coast marked with a ring in the Count's English atlas.

Whitby is a place on the Yorkshire coast, marked with a ring in an atlas the narrator sees in Count Dracula's library. It is one of three ringed locations, alongside Exeter and a spot near London. A letter from the Count is addressed to Samuel F. Billington at No. 7, The Crescent, Whitby.

Whitby is a seaside town on the Yorkshire coast, set in a steep river valley with red-roofed houses climbing above a harbour, and it has a ruined abbey and a churchyard on the cliff above. Lucy and Mina go there, and Mina lodges with Lucy at a house on The Crescent. The town is described as a lovely place with a view over the harbour toward the headland of Kettleness.

Whitby is a seaside town on the Yorkshire coast, set in a deep river valley with red-roofed houses stacked above a harbour, and crowned by a ruined abbey and a churchyard on the cliff. Mina writes of it as a lovely place, and Lucy is staying there with her mother, with Mina lodging with them at The Crescent. A stormy night is later reported from it, with a harbour and piers, and the view ranges to the headland of Kettleness. The Count has marked it on his atlas, and he has written to a Samuel F. Billington at No. 7, The Crescent, Whitby.

Whitby is an old seaside town on the Yorkshire coast, with a river valley, red-roofed houses stacked above a harbour, a ruined abbey and a churchyard on the cliff. Lucy and her mother are staying there, and Mina lodges with them at The Crescent. The Count has marked it on his atlas and addressed a letter to Samuel F. Billington at No. 7, The Crescent.

Whitby is an old seaside town on the Yorkshire coast, with red-roofed houses piled above a harbour, a river valley, and a ruined abbey and churchyard on the cliff. Lucy and her mother stay there at The Crescent, where Mina joins them. The Count has marked it on his atlas and addressed a letter to Samuel F. Billington at No. 7, The Crescent, Whitby.

Whitby is an old seaside town on the Yorkshire coast, with red-roofed houses stacked above a harbour and a river valley running down to it. A ruined abbey and a churchyard sit on the cliff above, and Lucy and her mother lodge there at The Crescent. The Count has ringed it on his atlas and addressed a letter to Samuel F. Billington at No. 7, The Crescent, Whitby.
A Whitby solicitor of 7, The Crescent, to whom the Demeter's cargo of boxes of mould was consigned. He formally took possession of the goods.
Acted as solicitor sending instructions to Carter, Paterson & Co. for delivering the boxes to Carfax.

Samuel F. Billington is a Whitby solicitor with an office-style address at No. 7, The Crescent. He is the consignee of a cargo of wooden boxes of mould from the Russian schooner Demeter, and he formally takes possession of those goods. A letter from the Count is addressed to him.

Samuel F. Billington is a Whitby solicitor whose office is at No. 7, The Crescent. He is the named consignee of the mould-filled wooden boxes from the Russian schooner Demeter, and he formally takes possession of them. He is the senior partner of the firm Samuel F. Billington & Son, which writes to a London carrier, Carter, Paterson & Co., urging speed in their business. A letter from the Count is addressed to him.
The port from which the Russian schooner Demeter sailed.
Varna is a port city, the place a Russian schooner, the Demeter, sailed from. It is named as the home town of a banker's correspondent, Herr Leutner, and as the origin of the ship's voyage to Whitby.

Varna is a port city on the sea, the place from which a Russian schooner, the Demeter, set sail. It is the home town of Herr Leutner, a correspondent of bankers, and the starting point of the ship's voyage to Whitby.

Varna is a port city on the sea, the place from which the Russian schooner Demeter departed. Herr Leutner is connected to it as someone living there, and it is where the Czarina Catherine is bound. Its harbour is also where a box of earth is to be delivered to an agent named Ristics.

Varna is a Black Sea port city, a place of harbour and shipping where the Russian schooner Demeter sailed from and where the Czarina Catherine is bound. It is where the box of earth is to be landed and handed to an agent named Ristics. The companions plan to travel there overland to meet the ship.

Varna is a Black Sea port city, a harbour town of shipping and trade. The Russian schooner Demeter sailed from it, and the Czarina Catherine is bound for it. The box of earth is to be landed there and handed to an agent named Ristics, and the companions plan to travel overland to meet the ship there.
The fairest of three women with golden wavy hair and pale sapphire eyes, who seems strangely known to Harker.

The fair woman is one of the female vampires, the Un-Dead, who preys on a man by lingering over him with a hungry, sensual manner. She has fair hair, blue eyes and scarlet lips, and she is shown in the company of the Count, who violently hurls her away from a victim and forbids the others to touch him.

The bag is a dark, mysterious sack that the man who carries it throws onto the floor, and it seems to move as if something living is inside. Its contents are a frightened, half-smothered child. Later, the professor uses it to carry his own tools and a candle, and he also keeps the professor's things in it.
Gipsies of the region, allied to ordinary gipsies, who attach themselves to a great noble and camp at the castle.

The Szgany are a band of gipsies, a people peculiar to this part of the world and tied to Hungary and Transylvania. They attach themselves to a great noble or boyar and take his name. They are fearless, have no religion beyond superstition, and speak their own varieties of the Romany tongue. Their hetman leads them, and they arrive with wagons and labour of their own.

The Szgany are a band of gipsies, a people peculiar to this part of the world and tied to Hungary and Transylvania. They attach themselves to a great noble or boyar and take his name. They are fearless, have no religion beyond superstition, and speak their own varieties of the Romany tongue. Their hetman leads them, and they arrive with wagons and labour of their own.

Wolves are a pack of wild animals in the mountains around the Count's castle, appearing as ring-like, silent, or howling groups. They are lean and shaggy with white teeth and red tongues, and they respond to the Count's commanding gesture and call. They are described as children of the night, and they are present at the castle gates.

Wolves are a pack of wild animals in the mountains around the Count's castle, traveling in howling groups or silent rings. They have lean, shaggy bodies, white teeth and red tongues, and respond to the Count's commanding gesture and call. They are called children of the night, and they gather at the castle courtyard.

Wolves are a wild pack haunting the mountains around the Count's ruined castle, howling in distant chorus or gathering in silent rings. They have lean, long-limbed, shaggy bodies, white teeth and lolling red tongues, and they answer the Count's commanding gesture and call. The Count names them the children of the night, and they pour into the castle courtyard at his summons.
Lucy is Mina's close friend, prone to sleepwalking; she wanders out at night and is found asleep on the seat in the churchyard.
Is pale, weak, short of breath, with a sore throat, and has frightening dreams she cannot recall.
Gravely weakened, pale and struggling to breathe, she is in need of blood transfusion.
Has recovered strength after several days of care and no longer fears sleep.
Her breathing and voice change into a voluptuous, hard-eyed state; her teeth look longer and sharper, and she has died.
Clutches garlic flowers when awake and pushes them away when in her stertorous sleep.
The wounds on her throat have vanished.
Appears in death with a radiant beauty, red lips and a bloom on her cheeks, and her sharpened teeth are longer than before.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman who writes letters to Mina Murray, confiding in her about her feelings and her suitors. She is warm, lively and quick to tears, and she is open about her affections. She has several admirers, including Dr. Seward, Mr. Quincey P. Morris, and a man named Arthur, whom she is close to.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman and a close friend of Mina Murray, to whom she writes candid letters about her romantic life. She is lively, sweet-natured and quick to tears, and older people warm to her readily. She has several admirers, including Dr. Seward and Mr. Quincey P. Morris, and is close to a man named Arthur Holmwood. She has a habit of walking in her sleep, which her mother says her late father also had.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman and close friend of Mina Murray, to whom she writes candid letters about her romantic life. She is sweet, lively and quick to tears, with a rosy colour that grows fresher at Whitby, and older people warm to her readily. She has several admirers, including Dr. Seward and Mr. Quincey P. Morris, and is close to Arthur Holmwood. She still walks in her sleep, a habit her mother says her late husband also had.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman and close friend of Mina Murray, to whom she writes candid letters about her romantic life. She is sweet, lively and quick to tears, and older people readily take to her. She has several admirers, including Quincey P. Morris and Dr. Seward, and is close to Arthur Holmwood. Her colour has grown rosier at Whitby, though she still walks in her sleep, a habit her mother says her late husband also had.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman and close friend of Mina Murray, and the daughter of Mrs. Westenra. She is sweet, lively and quick to tears, and older people readily warm to her. Her colour has grown rosier, though she sleepwalks and is later said to be weakening, and her engagement to Arthur Holmwood is mentioned.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman and close friend of Mina Murray, and the daughter of Mrs. Westenra. She is lively and sweet, quick to tears, with rosy cheeks that later fade, and she walks in her sleep. Her engagement to the Hon. Arthur Holmwood is mentioned, and she is said to be growing weaker.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman, a close friend of Mina Murray and the daughter of Mrs. Westenra. She is lively and warm in manner, quick to tears, and walks in her sleep. Her engagement to Arthur Holmwood is mentioned, and her health declines sharply, leaving her very pale and weak.
Young, strong and devoted to Lucy, and willing to give his blood to save her.
Inherits the whole Westenra estate, except a small entailed property, after Mrs. Westenra's will was made.
Grieving Lucy's death and the loss of his father; the Westenra estate now belongs to him.
Feels that through the transfusion he and Lucy were truly married in the sight of God.
Van Helsing judges that Arthur must pass through a bitter ordeal and that the truth about Lucy would grieve him terribly.

Arthur is a young man of good birth and wealth, called the Hon. Arthur Holmwood, who is loved by Lucy and is a close friend of Quincey P. Morris. Lucy describes him as someone who speaks little slang and never tells stories, and he is the person she has told Mina she is in love with, though he has not said so in words.

Arthur Holmwood, styled the Hon. Arthur, is the only son of Lord Godalming and a young man of good birth and means. He is loved by Lucy, who is to marry him, and he is close to Quincey P. Morris, to whom he writes. Lucy says he speaks little slang and never tells stories, and his ill father is expected to recover.

Arthur Holmwood, styled the Hon. Arthur, is the only son of Lord Godalming and is engaged to Lucy Westenra. He is a young man of good birth and wealth who is close to Quincey P. Morris, to whom he writes. Lucy describes him as speaking little slang and rarely telling stories, and his father's illness keeps him often called away.

Arthur Holmwood, styled the Hon. Arthur, is the only son of Lord Godalming and is engaged to Lucy Westenra. He is a young man of good birth and wealth, well liked by Mina Murray, who notes that Lucy describes him as speaking little slang. He often calls on Lucy and her mother, is frequently summoned away by his ailing father, and gives his own blood to save Lucy in a transfusion, showing himself devoted and brave.

Arthur Holmwood, called the Hon. Arthur, is engaged to Lucy Westenra and is a well-born, wealthy young man. He often visits Lucy and her mother, is called away to attend his ailing father, and gives his blood in a transfusion to save Lucy. He is devoted to Lucy and is overcome with grief when she dies.

Arthur Holmwood, called the Hon. Arthur, is the only son of Lord Godalming and is engaged to Lucy Westenra. He is tall, curly-haired and well-born, and visits Lucy and her mother often. He is devoted to Lucy, gives his blood to save her, and is left grieving when she dies.

The Hon. Arthur Holmwood is the only son of Lord Godalming, and is loved by Lucy Westenra, who calls him Arthur. He is tall and curly-haired, visits Lucy and her mother often, and is a friend of Dr. Seward and Quincey Morris. He gives his blood to save Lucy and is grief-stricken when she dies.
Keeps a phonograph diary and works with patients, including Renfield, whom he studies closely.
Is a man of noble nature who keeps phonograph diary entries and gives Mina access to his records out of trust.
Doubts Renfield's sincerity, fearing he is tied to the Count and may try to help him in some diabolical way.

Dr. John Seward is a doctor who runs a lunatic asylum, with a strong jaw and a good forehead. He proposes to Lucy, who does not return his feelings, and he is recognised as an old friend of Quincey Morris, who invites him to a gathering.

Dr. John Seward is a doctor who runs a lunatic asylum and treats its patients, including Renfield, whose case he studies closely. He has a strong jaw and a good forehead, and is outwardly cool but nervous in company. He proposed to Lucy, who did not return his feelings, and is an old friend of Quincey Morris and Arthur Holmwood, whose father he treats for, and he calls on Van Helsing for help with Lucy's illness.

Dr. John Seward is a doctor who runs a lunatic asylum and keeps close watch on his patient Renfield, whose strange behaviour he records in his diary. He is cool and composed in outward manner, though nervous underneath, with a strong jaw and a good forehead. He proposed to Lucy Westenra, who did not return his love, and he is an old friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey Morris. He has called in his old master, Van Helsing, to help with Lucy's worsening illness, and sits up watching over her.

Dr. John Seward is a doctor who runs a lunatic asylum and keeps close watch over the patient Renfield, whose strange conduct he records in his diary. He is outwardly cool but nervous underneath, with a strong jaw and a good forehead. He proposed to Lucy Westenra, who did not return his love, and he is an old friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey Morris. He calls Abraham Van Helsing his old master and sits up watching over Lucy during her worsening illness.

Dr. John Seward runs a lunatic asylum and watches closely over the patient Renfield, whose strange conduct he records in his diary. He is cool on the surface yet nervous underneath, with a strong jaw and a good forehead. He once proposed to Lucy Westenra, who did not return his love, and he is an old friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey Morris. He calls Abraham Van Helsing his old master and sits up through the nights watching over Lucy during her failing health.

Dr. John Seward runs a lunatic asylum and keeps a diary of his observations of the patient Renfield. He is outwardly cool but inwardly nervous, with a strong jaw and a good forehead, and he once proposed to Lucy Westenra, who did not return his love. He is an old friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey Morris, calls Abraham Van Helsing his old master, and sat up watching over Lucy during her decline.

Dr. John Seward runs a lunatic asylum and keeps a diary of his observations of the patient Renfield. He is outwardly cool but inwardly nervous, with a strong jaw and a good forehead, and he once proposed to Lucy Westenra, who did not return his love. He is an old friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey Morris, calls Abraham Van Helsing his old master, and sat up watching over Lucy during her decline.

Mr. Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, a well-mannered, cheerful man who is nonetheless nervous when speaking to Lucy and fond of telling tales and playing with American slang in her company. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and of Jack Seward, and he proposes to Lucy, who tells him she loves another man. He writes warmly to Arthur, inviting him to a campfire gathering, and is described by Dr. Seward's notes as possibly dangerous if unselfish.

Mr. Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, outwardly young and fresh, cheerful and well mannered, who speaks American slang only in the company of those who will not be shocked. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, and he once proposed to Lucy, who told him she loved another man. He stays to help with Lucy's care, offering his blood for transfusion and patrolling the house through the night.

Mr. Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, young and fresh in appearance, cheerful and well mannered, who speaks slang only before those who won't be shocked. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, and once proposed to Lucy, who told him she loved another. He gives his blood for Lucy's transfusions, keeps watch over the house through the night, and is spoken of by Seward as a brave, steadfast man.

Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas who is young, fresh-looking and well mannered, and who speaks slang only before people he won't shock. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, and once proposed to Lucy, who told him she loved another. He gives blood for Lucy's transfusions, keeps watch over the house through the night, and is a steadfast, brave man who bears grief quietly.

Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, young and fresh-looking, well educated and mannerly, who uses slang only before people he is comfortable with. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, and once proposed to Lucy, who told him she loved another. He gives blood for Lucy's transfusions, patrols the house through the night, and stays steady and brave, bearing grief quietly.

Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, young-looking, well educated and mannerly, who uses slang only with people he is at ease with. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, and once proposed to Lucy. He gives blood for Lucy's transfusions, keeps watch over the house through the night, and stays brave and steady, bearing grief quietly and joining the group at the tomb.

Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, a close friend of Arthur and Jack Seward, who looks young and fresh. He is well educated and mannerly, using slang only when at ease, and he has offered blood for Lucy's transfusions. He keeps watch over the house by night, speaks plainly and loyally, and joins the group in pursuing the Count's earth-boxes and the tomb.
The journal kept by Dr. Seward, in which he records his observations of patients and his own thoughts.
A patient of Dr. Seward who shows selfish, secretive purpose and a cruel love of collecting and eating living creatures, which Seward sees as a homicidal, life-devouring mania.
Shows sudden religious mania, speaking of a coming Master and refusing to talk to attendants.
Immensely strong and violent in paroxysms; now chained to a wall in a padded room in a strait-waistcoat.
Speaks with lucid, courteous philosophical reasoning when Mina is present, though Seward finds this sudden change striking.
Admits to having once believed life could be prolonged by consuming living things and tried to kill Seward for his blood.
Speaks with unusual rational self-possession and claims his sanity, though Seward suspects it is another phase of his madness.
Speaks with courteous, dignified self-control and expresses gratitude to Seward when calm.
Dreads acquiring the soul of a human, suggesting he expects to gain some higher life.
Believes he is dying and speaks of a presence he calls He, which he says came to his window and made promises.

R. M. Renfield is a patient at an asylum, aged 59, with a sanguine temperament, great physical strength and a morbidly excitable nature. He is secretive and selfish, with a fixed purpose the doctor cannot yet make out, and he keeps animals he cruelly collects and destroys. The doctor, Dr. Seward, who keeps a diary, watches him closely.

R. M. Renfield is a patient at an asylum, aged 59, with a sanguine temperament, great physical strength and a morbidly excitable nature. He is secretive and selfish, with a fixed purpose the doctor cannot yet make out, and he keeps animals he cruelly collects and destroys. He has grown haughty and religiously fervent toward a figure he calls his Master, whom he serves as a faithful slave. Dr. Seward watches him closely, and he has escaped the asylum at night to an adjoining deserted house.

R. M. Renfield is an asylum patient, aged 59, with a sanguine temperament, great physical strength and a morbidly excitable nature. He is selfish, secretive and purposeful, keeps animals he collects and destroys, and has grown haughty and fervent toward a figure he calls his Master, whom he serves as a slave. He has twice slipped out at night to the deserted house beside the asylum grounds.

R. M. Renfield is an asylum patient, aged 59, with a sanguine temperament and great physical strength. He is selfish, secretive and purposeful, collects and destroys animals, and speaks of a figure he calls his Master, whom he serves as a slave. He has repeatedly slipped out at night to the deserted house beside the asylum grounds, and his outbursts seem linked to the nearby house.

R. M. Renfield is an asylum patient, aged 59, with a sanguine temperament and great physical strength. He is selfish, secretive and purposeful, and keeps collecting and killing small creatures such as flies, spiders and birds. He repeatedly slips out at night to the deserted house beside the asylum grounds, calling someone he serves his Master and claiming to be a slave to that Master.

R. M. Renfield is an asylum patient aged 59, with a sanguine temperament and great physical strength. He is selfish, secretive and purposeful, and collects and kills small creatures such as flies, spiders and birds. He repeatedly escapes at night to the deserted house beside the grounds, calling someone he serves his Master and claiming to be that Master's slave.

Kettleness is a headland that stretches out into the sea beyond Whitby's harbour, seen from the churchyard above the town. It is a steep, grey rock formation, and a place where a man named George Canon is said to have fallen to his death, according to an inscription on a tombstone.

Kettleness is a headland that juts out into the sea north of Whitby's harbour, seen from the churchyard above the town. It is a steep, dark mass that stands boldly against the western sky at sunset. A tombstone at its edge is inscribed with the fall of George Canon from its rocks in 1873, the cause of which is given there as a fall; local speakers dispute that account.

Mr. Swales is an elderly local man of Whitby, speaking in a thick regional dialect that the narrator only partly follows. He is a former sailor, with a sardonic, mocking manner that delights in exposing the gravestone inscriptions around the churchyard as lies. He keeps company with a group of older cronies who laugh along with him, and he is quick to talk to the narrator.
The title by which Arthur Holmwood is referred to, now Lucy's fiancé and heir to the Westenra estate.

Lord Godalming is the father of Arthur Holmwood, and is described as a close friend of Mrs. Westenra. He is ill and not well, and is absent at Ring for much of the time. His name is spoken by the solicitor and others, but no traits of his own are shown in the passages.

Lord Godalming is the father of Arthur Holmwood, the Hon. Arthur, and is ill, so he is away at Ring while his son is in Whitby. He is a dear friend of Mrs. Westenra, and the solicitor says he would have had no claim on her estate. Van Helsing says he is a friend of Lord Godalming and has been empowered by him to read Lucy's letters and papers, and he is in some way tied to Arthur as the one who was Lucy's fiancé.

Lord Godalming is the title held by the father of the Hon. Arthur Holmwood, and he is in poor health, so he is away at Ring for much of this stretch. He is a close friend of Mrs. Westenra and of Van Helsing's circle, and Van Helsing says Lord Godalming has empowered him to read Lucy's letters and papers. The title passes to Arthur, Lucy's former fiancé, and Lord Godalming himself is the one who gave Van Helsing that permission.

Lord Godalming is the Hon. Arthur Holmwood's father, a peer whose poor health keeps him at Ring for a long stretch. He is a close friend of Mrs. Westenra, and the passages say Van Helsing was empowered by Lord Godalming to read Lucy's letters and papers. Lord Godalming is not named as the title-holder by the solicitor; the passages show him as a dear friend of the late Mrs. Westenra.

Lord Godalming is the father of the Hon. Arthur Holmwood, and a dear friend of the late Mrs. Westenra. He is in poor health, and in this passage is at Ring, away from town. Van Helsing says he was empowered by Lord Godalming to read Lucy's letters and papers. Lord Godalming is addressed as a member of the group joining the council against the vampire.

Lord Godalming is the father of the Hon. Arthur Holmwood, and is a dear friend of the late Mrs. Westenra. He is in poor health and, in these passages, has been called to Ring to see him, away from town. Van Helsing says Lord Godalming has empowered him to read Lucy's letters and papers. Lord Godalming is also named as a member of the group joining the council against the vampire.

Lord Godalming is the father of the Hon. Arthur Holmwood and a dear friend of the late Mrs. Westenra. He is frail in health and lives at Ring, where his son is often summoned to attend him. Van Helsing says Lord Godalming has empowered him to read Lucy's letters and papers, and Lord Godalming joins the group that pledges itself against the vampire, saying he does so for Lucy's sake.
Ring is a place, named as where Arthur Holmwood's father lives and where he is called to attend him during an illness. Letters and telegrams are to be directed there to reach Holmwood.
A coastguard at Whitby who keeps a spy-glass and chats with Mina. He watches the strange ship closely.

The coastguard is a watchman on duty at the harbour, who keeps a spy-glass and talks with the narrator as he patrols. He is observant and practical, reading the behaviour of a strange ship. Later he is the first to board a derelict vessel and examines the steering wheel, and he works as one of the coastguards on duty on the harbour's eastern side.
A high ground at Whitby with a churchyard that overlooks the sea.

East Cliff is a high headland above Whitby harbour, with a churchyard along its edge that gives a wide view over the sea. Local watchers, including an old fisherman, use it to study the weather. A searchlight is set up on its summit during the storm, and it overlooks Tate Hill Pier, where a schooner runs aground beneath it.

East Cliff is a high headland above Whitby harbour, topped by the old churchyard and its wide view over the sea. Local watchers use it to read the weather, and a searchlight is set up on its summit during the storm. Across the harbour from the West Cliff, it is a favourite seat for two young women who walk there, and it lies beside the ruined abbey and St. Mary's Church.
A steamer that makes trips up and down the coast from Whitby on holiday days.
A wooded place near Whitby that holiday-makers visit.

Mulgrave Woods is a place near Whitby, a spot holiday-makers visit for outings from the town. Mrs. Westenra drives there by road while Lucy and the narrator walk the cliff-path to join her at its gate, and the group takes its lunch there on a bright day.
A bay near Whitby that holiday-makers visit.
A bay near Whitby, reached by a walk along the cliffs, where holiday-makers go.
A coastal village near Whitby that holiday-makers visit.
A steamer that makes trips up and down the coast from Whitby on holiday days.
A coastal village near Whitby that holiday-makers visit.
A pier at Whitby harbour mouth, below the churchyard cliff.

East Pier is a stone harbour mole at Whitby, on the far side of the harbour mouth from the searchlight. It is the wall ships must pass between to reach safety, and the place where a runaway schooner was expected to strike. Its lane runs beneath the churchyard on the eastern cliff.
A small pier in Whitby harbour where the strange schooner ran aground.

Tate Hill Pier is a small pier in Whitby harbour, known locally by that name for the heap of sand and gravel that collects in its south-east corner under the East Cliff. It is a landing place near the homes of those who live close by, and it is where the wrecked schooner Demeter runs aground in the storm and where the dead steersman is taken off. Its surroundings include the churchyard above and the East Cliff.
A foreign schooner with all sails set that drove into Whitby harbour with a dead man lashed to its wheel.
A figure of steadfast duty mentioned by the correspondent as a comparison for the dead steersman.
The official body whose inspectors examined the wrecked schooner and its log-book in Whitby.

The Board of Trade is an official body whose inspectors oversee ship matters at Whitby. Its officials are exacting, insisting that every regulation is followed for the derelict schooner. One inspector allows the narrator to examine the Demeter's log-book.
A Russian schooner from Varna, largely in ballast of silver sand, carrying great wooden boxes of mould, that was wrecked in Whitby harbour.

Demeter is a Russian schooner out of Varna, found drifting into Whitby harbour during a storm. It is carrying mostly silver sand as ballast, plus a small cargo of wooden boxes of mould consigned to a local solicitor. Its log and a paper found in a bottle are part of the record surrounding it.
Official who acted for the charter-party and took formal possession of the ship in Whitby.

The Russian consul is an official who acts for the charter-party in Whitby, formally taking possession of the schooner Demeter and paying its harbour dues. He has a clerk who translates for the narrator, and the narrator writes that the consul kindly helped with the translation. Nothing more of his appearance or manner is shown.
The animal protection society, strong in Whitby, whose members tried to befriend the landed dog.
A London carrying firm hired to transport a large consignment of boxes from King's Cross to Carfax, delivering them as instructed.

Carter, Paterson & Co. is a London firm that receives and delivers goods, and it corresponds in writing with the Whitby solicitors Samuel F. Billington & Son. It replies through a clerk acting for the firm, acknowledging payment, returning an overplus cheque, and confirming that goods were delivered as instructed and keys left in the main hall.
The railway company by which the consignment of goods is sent to King's Cross.

names.value: Hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary

facets.text: A hospital in Buda-Pesth where Jonathan Harker was nursed for a brain fever.
A nurse at the Hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary in Buda-Pesth who writes letters on behalf of her patients. Kind and devout in tone.

Sister Agatha is a nun at the Hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary in Buda-Pesth, where she nurses patients. She writes with warmth and sympathy, and she has been caring for Jonathan Harker, who is recovering from a violent brain fever. She writes on Jonathan's behalf to his employer, Mr. Peter Hawkins, and passes news on to Miss Wilhelmina Murray.

Sister Agatha is a nun at the Hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary in Buda-Pesth, where she nurses Jonathan Harker through his illness. She writes with warmth and sympathy, and she tends the sick with a kind, devout manner. She is described as a good, sweet soul and a born nurse, who keeps the confidences of her patients and will not repeat their ravings.

Hillingham is the home of Lucy Westenra and her mother, Mrs. Westenra, where Lucy has been brought back to after a stay away. It is a quiet house in which Lucy grows steadily weaker, and it is where Arthur and Dr. Jack Seward visit her and where Van Helsing examines her.

Hillingham is the quiet home of Lucy Westenra and her mother, Mrs. Westenra, and Lucy is brought back there after time away. It is where Lucy grows weaker, where Arthur and Dr. Jack Seward visit her, and where Van Helsing examines her. Lucy's maids are devoted to her there, and she is later seen improving under care.
The London hotel where Arthur Holmwood writes his letter to Seward.

Amsterdam is a city where Professor Van Helsing lives and works. Dr. Seward relies on him as an old friend and master, a physician who knows obscure diseases and is said to be deeply learned. Seward sends telegrams there, and Van Helsing returns to Amsterdam after visiting Hillingham.

Amsterdam is a city where Professor Van Helsing lives and works, and he travels there and back as needed. Dr. Seward calls Van Helsing his old friend and master, a physician knowledgeable about obscure diseases. Seward sends telegrams to Van Helsing there.

Amsterdam is the city where Professor Van Helsing lives, and he travels back and forth between it and London as needed. Dr. Seward calls Van Helsing his old friend and master, and Van Helsing is said to have taught Seward when Seward studied there. Van Helsing goes there to fetch books and other things he needs.
Advises discretion, keeping knowledge and his own thoughts from those who are not needed, and keeping careful records.
Shows deep despair and religious anguish when the situation worsens, then rallies to act against the evil.
Asks Arthur to trust him without yet explaining, promising understanding later.
Speaks from ancient lore and his experience of the Un-Dead, insisting the staking is a blessing that frees the soul of the dead.
Gives Seward typewritten copies of Harker's and Mina's diaries and urges careful reading and an open mind.
Admits he would have released Renfield earlier, and reasons that in their present task no chances may be taken.
Pores over the Harkers' records in Seward's study, hoping accurate knowledge of every detail will yield a clue.
Argues the group should wait for full daylight and act lawfully, to avoid suspicion, when searching houses.
Reasons that the Count is fleeing by ship, that the group can rest because he cannot cross the water, and that they must follow him.
Believes Mina's trance has given him a way to hinder the Count, and hides from her the fact that she was in a trance.
Travels tirelessly by carriage, hurrying the group onward while paying farmers for horses.
Grows fearful and uneasy as Mina's sleep and unusual health continue, though he hides his fear from her.

Abraham Van Helsing is a learned doctor of Amsterdam, described as an old friend and former master of Dr. Seward, and he knows a great deal about obscure diseases. He is a philosopher, metaphysician and advanced scientist, with an iron nerve, an unbending resolve, a blunt manner and a warm, kind heart. He is called to attend Lucy Westenra, and he reads her condition as likely having a mental cause rather than a physical one.

Abraham Van Helsing is a learned doctor and professor from Amsterdam, and an old master of Dr. Seward who knows much about obscure diseases. He is a philosopher, metaphysician and advanced scientist with an iron nerve, a blunt, commanding manner and a kindly heart. He treats Lucy Westenra, performs blood transfusions on her, and uses garlic and narcotics in her care.

Abraham Van Helsing is an elderly Amsterdam doctor and professor, an old master of Dr. Seward who knows much about obscure diseases. He is a philosopher, metaphysician and advanced scientist with an iron nerve, a blunt, stern, commanding manner, and a kindly heart. He treats Lucy Westenra, performs blood transfusions on her, uses narcotics and garlic in her care, and insists his orders be obeyed.

Abraham Van Helsing is an elderly Amsterdam doctor and professor, an old master of Dr. Seward who knows much about obscure diseases. He is a stern, commanding man of iron nerve and a kindly heart, a philosopher, metaphysician and advanced scientist who treats Lucy Westenra with narcotics, garlic and blood transfusions. He insists his orders be obeyed and is regarded as one who knows more than anyone else.

Abraham Van Helsing is an elderly Amsterdam professor and old master of Dr. Seward, known for his knowledge of obscure diseases. He is stern and commanding, with an iron nerve and a kindly, true heart, and he is a philosopher and advanced scientist who insists his orders be obeyed. He treats Lucy Westenra with narcotics, garlic, and blood transfusions, and he is carefully methodical, even in grief.

Abraham Van Helsing is an elderly professor from Amsterdam, the old master of Dr. Seward and a expert in obscure diseases. He is a stern, commanding man with an iron nerve and a kindly, true heart, a philosopher and advanced scientist who insists his orders be followed. He treats Lucy Westenra with narcotics, garlic, flowers, and blood transfusions, and works with careful, methodical resolve even in grief.

Abraham Van Helsing is an elderly Amsterdam professor, the old teacher and friend of Dr. Seward, and an expert in obscure diseases. He is a stern, commanding man of iron nerve and a kindly, true heart, a philosopher and advanced scientist who insists on his own orders. He works with methodical, unhurried care, performing blood transfusions and watching over Lucy Westenra with resolve, and he carries consecrated objects against the dead.
A patient of Dr. Seward's asylum who eats living creatures such as flies and is closely watched by the doctor.
A patient of Dr. Seward's asylum who is kept under close watch by the doctor.
Is the sane-seeming lunatic who spoke of consuming live things, and whose mouth held flies and spiders just before Mrs. Harker entered.
Lucy has grown fond of it, and a boxful is sent to her each day from Haarlem.

Garlic appears as a common flower-like herb that is hung and strewn about a room and worn in a wreath. Van Helsing has it sent from Haarlem, where it is grown in glass-houses, and treats it as protective. Lucy takes it for an ordinary joke at first, though it is presented as something with real virtue against unseen danger.

Garlic is a common herb with small flowers, grown in glass-houses at Haarlem and sent over in boxes. Van Helsing treats it as a protection, hanging it about rooms and making it into a wreath for Lucy to wear, and Lucy first takes it for a joke but later finds its smell soothing.

Garlic is a common herb with small flowers, grown in glass-houses at Haarlem and sent over in boxes. Van Helsing uses it as a guard against the Un-Dead, hanging it in rooms, making a wreath for Lucy to wear, and placing it on her coffin and at her tomb. Lucy first mocks it as ordinary, then finds its smell soothing and clutches it when she wakes.
The newspaper whose interviewer is writing up the escaped wolf story.

The Pall Mall Gazette is a newspaper whose name a reporter uses as a talisman to win the cooperation of people he approaches. Its interviewer seeks out a zoo keeper for a story about an escaped wolf. The passages show nothing more about the paper itself.
A keeper at the Zoölogical Gardens who knows the animals from long experience, cheerful and blunt, and fond of the wolf Bersicker.

Thomas Bilder is a keeper at the Zoölogical Gardens, in charge of the wolf section, and lives in a cottage behind the elephant-house with his wife. He is elderly, childless, hospitable, and speaks in a broad working-class dialect. He is blunt and good-humoured, fond of joking, and tender toward the wolf Bersicker, whom he treats like a pet.
A grey wolf from Norway, bought from Jamrach's four years ago, usually well behaved and seldom troublesome. He escapes his enclosure in the Zoölogical Gardens after being disturbed by a stranger.
Returns to the Zoo on his own, cut on the head from broken glass, and is locked back in his cage.

Bersicker is a grey wolf, one of three brought from Norway to Jamrach's and bought by the keeper's employer; the keeper calls it a nice, well-behaved animal. It is known for tearing at its bars and for escaping its cage, and it is later found back at the menagerie with a cut head. It is tended by the keeper Bilder.
The dealer from whom the Zoölogical Gardens bought the grey wolves four years earlier.
Thomas Bilder's wife, cheerful and hospitable, who lives with him at the Zoölogical Gardens.
A man Van Helsing plans to look up in the search for the missing earth-boxes.

Thomas Snelling is one of two carriers, employed by Harris & Sons Moving and Shipment Company, who clash with the patient Renfield at an empty house. He is a rough, unbothered man who takes a blow to the head without seeming to mind it, and he is later sought out by Harker. His address is given as Peter Farley's Row, Guide Court, Bethnal Green.
An obsequious, urbane undertaker who arranges the funeral and the viewing rooms for Lucy and her mother.

The undertaker is a tradesman who handles the coffin and preparations after a death, and he and his men are summoned to the house. The passages do not give him a name, look, or manner beyond his work, and his men are only mentioned as carrying out his preparations.
The solicitors' firm to which Mr. Marquand belongs, which handled Mrs. Westenra's affairs.
President of the Incorporated Law Society, represented at Mr. Hawkins's funeral by a gentleman.

Sir John Paxton is a name that appears in two places: once as a drowned mariner listed by an old local, and once as the President of the Incorporated Law Society, whom a gentleman represents at a funeral service. Beyond these two ties, the passages say little more about him as a person.
Van Helsing's personified name for laughter that comes unbidden, even in grief.

King Laugh is a figure Van Helsing invokes as a personified force: a sovereign who arrives unbidden and whenever he pleases, bringing mirth even amid grief, and who has left Van Helsing for a long time. He is described as one who makes sorrows dance to his tune.
A hill near Lucy's resting place, over which the sun rises.
The phrase children use to describe the woman who lured them away on the Heath.

The bloofer lady is a figure in the children's talk around Hampstead Heath, the name they give to whoever they say lured them away. The passages never show her directly; she is only described through children's excuses for being missing. Several are said to have been wounded in the throat, though nothing confirms who or what she is.
A heath near Hampstead where children have been going missing and returning wounded in the throat.

Hampstead Heath is an open stretch of land where young children go to play and where several have been lost, found late or hurt. Its quieter parts, such as the Shooter's Hill side with its furze bushes, are less often visited. The children found after going missing say they were with a "bloofer lady", and some have small wounds in the throat that may have come from an animal.
Lucy's diary, kept in shorthand after Mina left Whitby, which Mina shows to Van Helsing.

Paddington is a London railway station, the terminus where trains from Exeter arrive. It appears only as a destination on train timetables that characters discuss, so it serves as a place of arrival rather than a person.
A scientist, now deceased, whose work on hypnotism Van Helsing and Harker discuss.

Dr. Vincent is a doctor at the North Hospital, where a child who has been bitten is being treated. He is a friend of Van Helsing and had studied in Amsterdam under him, and he examines the child's wounds and offers a theory that a bat or an escaped animal caused them.
The family tomb in the churchyard where Lucy's coffin was laid, now opened by Van Helsing.
A church dispensation Van Helsing says he holds, which he invokes as he uses sacred things against the Un-Dead.
The consecrated wafer Van Helsing brought from Amsterdam and uses to seal the tomb against the Un-Dead.
A small fair-haired child taken from its home by the Un-Dead Lucy and left in the churchyard, unharmed.

A small boy found in the North Hospital with two bite-like punctures on his throat, the same kind seen on Lucy. He is awake and recovering there, is brought from the churchyard by the narrators, and is left for a policeman to find on Hampstead Heath. He is said to have wanted to play with the 'bloofer lady'.
A London station reached by Underground from Paddington, on the way to Seward's asylum.

Fenchurch Street is a place, a London railway station the characters reach by Underground. It is also the site of a lunatic asylum, a fact the narrator says Mrs. Harker already knows. The passages show it only as a destination and a place near the Green Park, not with any further character.
A recording device on which Seward keeps his diary entries.

The phonograph is a recording device that Dr. Seward uses to keep his personal diary, speaking his entries into it and storing them on wax cylinders. Lucy Westenra also left a memorandum recorded on one, and Seward later passes its cylinders to Mina Harker to hear and transcribe. It is a cutting-edge, unfamiliar machine to Mina, who finds it fascinating.

The phonograph is a recording machine that Dr. Seward uses to keep his diary, speaking entries onto wax cylinders. It also holds a memorandum left by Lucy Westenra, and Seward gives its cylinders to Mina Harker to hear and transcribe. Mina finds the device new and fascinating, and it is the only copy of certain records kept in the safe.
Swarming rats that fill the old house and chapel, driven off by the dogs and Lord Godalming's whistle.

Rats are small rodents that Renfield, a patient, speaks of in a frenzied account, describing thousands of them with blazing red eyes that gather at a dark master's command. Renfield dismisses them as trivial 'chicken-feed' compared with larger prey. The rats are shown obeying a figure that Renfield serves, and they are described as coming on in a dark mass.
Keys used by the party to open the locked door of the house.
The chapel in the castle where Van Helsing finds the tombs of the Un-Dead women and does his work.

Chapel is the old chapel, a disused, dark place within the grounds of Carfax, reached by a winding stair and a dark passage from the Count's room. It holds the great boxes of earth, and it is where the Count's coffin-like boxes lie and where the Count himself is found, gorged with blood. Its air feels oppressive and sulphurous.
Bulky boxes of earth, fifty in number at first, now only twenty-nine remain at the house.
Three dogs belonging to Dr. Seward's household that come running at Lord Godalming's whistle and hunt the rats.

The attendants are the asylum's male staff who restrain patients and carry out Dr. Seward's orders. They are unnamed in general, though Hardy is one of them and has a finger broken during a struggle with Renfield. They follow Seward's instructions to watch, pursue, and restrain the patient, and they hold him when he is violent.
A reliable workman and mate, one of the two cart-men who once carried boxes from Carfax, with a notebook of destinations.

Joseph Smollet is a London carrier and workman who, with his mate Thomas Snelling, moved heavy wooden boxes from Carfax. He is the responsible person of the two mates, so Snelling is his assistant. He is described as decent, intelligent and reliable, with a practical headpiece and a dog's-eared notebook recording the box destinations.
A street in Poplar where a new cold storage building was being erected.
The Piccadilly house, where the Count's effects, title deeds and house keys are kept in the dining-room.
A hatch in the patient's door through which staff look in on him.
The Death's-head Moth, a moth Van Helsing names when Renfield describes moths with skull markings.
A passing policeman who nods acquiescence to the locksmith's work at the door.
The vampire Count Dracula, the group's enemy, whose lair and possessions the company is searching.
Left London by ship on the Czarina Catherine, with his box, and is believed to be heading for the Danube mouth and Transylvania.
Believed by the group to be strong, subtle and cunning, and able to sleep for a century if he escapes them.

Count Dracula is the nobleman of a remote Carpathian district who hosts Jonathan Harker in his castle. He is a boyar of marked appearance, with a great white moustache, who keeps no visible servants and seems to do the menial work himself. He has an unnatural strength and control over wolves and horses, casts no reflection in a mirror, and shows fury at the sight of a crucifix.

Count Dracula is the Carpathian nobleman and boyar who hosts Harker in his castle. He has a great white moustache, an unnaturally strong grip, and a commanding, ancient pride in his Szekely line. He keeps no servants and does the menial work himself, casts no reflection in glass, and can command wolves.
A sailing ship bound for Varna and up the Danube, which the group traces as the vessel carrying the Count's box.
A ship that left the Thames carrying the Count's box, bound for Varna, as the group understands it.

The Czarina Catherine is a sailing ship bound for Varna and the Black Sea, sailing from Doolittle's Wharf on the Thames. The men in the passages discuss her departure and route, and she is the vessel that the group believes carries the box in question.

The Czarina Catherine is a sailing ship on which the group believes the Count's box is being carried. She sails from Doolittle's Wharf on the Thames for Varna and the Black Sea, and the men track her passage by telegram. Her departure and progress are reported to Lloyd's and relayed to Lord Godalming.

The Czarina Catherine is a sailing ship that carries a sealed box, believed to hold Count Dracula's coffin-like cargo, on its voyage from London toward the Black Sea. Her passage is tracked through telegrams to Lloyd's and relayed to Lord Godalming, and she is described as swift and favoured by unusually steady winds and fog. She is reported at the Dardanelles and then at Galatz, where her cargo is cleared and handed to a local man, Skinsky.
A London wharf from which the Czarina Catherine sails for the Black Sea.
The shipping register where the group finds notes of every ship that sails, however small.
The shipping register to which Lord Godalming's agent telegraphs about whether the ship has been reported.
Repeating rifles Quincey Morris proposes the group add to its armament for the journey.

Winchesters are repeating rifles, weapons Quincey Morris proposes adding to the group's arms for the journey to Varna. He trusts them in dangerous situations with wolves, and Van Helsing agrees to take them along. Nothing else about them is given.

Winchesters are repeating rifles carried by the men in the group. Quincey Morris proposes adding them to their arms, and Van Helsing agrees. Morris trusts them in a crowd and against wolves. Later, the group uses them to cover the gypsies, who then stop resisting.
A Lloyd's agent in London who telegraphs shipping reports about the Czarina Catherine to Lord Godalming.

Rufus Smith is a correspondent in London, at Lloyd's, who sends telegrams to Lord Godalming in care of the Vice-Consul at Varna. The two telegrams concern the ship Czarina Catherine, reporting its progress from the Dardanelles and then its arrival at Galatz. He is not otherwise described.
A person who had been told to remove the crate and carry it off before dawn at Galatz.

Immanuel Hildesheim is a businessman in Galatz who runs an office and deals in money and shipping arrangements. He is described as a Hebrew with a sheep-like nose who wears a fez, and he works for pay. He received and handed over a box from the ship Czarina Catherine, having been instructed by letter.

Petrof Skinsky is a man who deals with the Slovak traders moving goods down the river to the port at Galatz. He is hired by an intermediary to collect a box from a local businessman, and he is later found dead, his throat torn open, outside a churchyard wall. His neighbours show him no affection.
A protective ring of sacred objects within which Mina and the narrator stand safe from the Un-Dead.

The Holy circle is a protective ring that stays around Madam Mina while she sleeps, keeping out the three women and the mist-figures who would draw her in. Those inside it cannot be reached by these creatures, and Mina cannot leave it, nor can they enter. Dr. Van Helsing leaves her inside it and later crosses it freely.
A consecrated object used as a protection against the Un-Dead, laid in Dracula's tomb to banish him.

The Wafer is a consecrated host, a piece of sacred bread used as a holy protection. Van Helsing places it on Mina's forehead, where it burns her skin, and he also carries pieces of it as a weapon against the vampire women. It repels the undead, keeping them outside a holy circle and banishing Dracula from his tomb.
